title: Reading the Parables
summary: What a parable is, the parables of the Old Testament and the rabbis, how Jesus used his, the hard saying about parables that conceal, and the long history of interpretation from the church fathers' allegories to Jülicher, Dodd, Jeremias, and the scholars of today, with a table of the parables and practical guidance for reading them.

sections.body:
Jesus taught in parables more than in any other way. Mark says that “He did not tell them anything without using a parable” (Mark 4:34), and roughly a third of his recorded teaching in the first three Gospels takes this form. The parables are among the best-known stories in the world; phrases such as ‘good Samaritan’ and ‘prodigal son’ have entered languages far from Christianity. Yet they are also among the most misread parts of the Bible, and the history of their interpretation is a history of learning how to read them.

The English word comes from the Greek parabolē, literally a ‘placing beside’: something set next to something else so that one illuminates the other. The Greek translators of the Old Testament used parabolē for the Hebrew mashal, which covers a wide range: proverbs, taunts, riddles, allegories, and stories. The New Testament uses the word just as broadly. A proverb can be called a parable, as when Jesus quotes ‘Physician, heal yourself’ (Luke 4:23), and so can a single comparison (the kingdom is like leaven) or a full story (a man had two sons).

Scholars commonly distinguish several kinds. Similitudes are short comparisons from everyday life, often in the present tense: “The kingdom of heaven is like treasure hidden in a field.” (Matthew 13:44). Narrative parables tell a particular story in the past tense: the lost son, the workers in the vineyard. Example stories give a model of conduct to follow or avoid: the Good Samaritan, the rich fool, the Pharisee and the tax collector. Some scholars add allegories, stories in which several details stand for something else, and debate how many of Jesus' parables belong there. Because the definitions differ, counts of Jesus' parables range from about thirty to more than sixty.

C. H. Dodd, in The Parables of the Kingdom (1935), offered a definition that many still cite. In summary: a parable is a metaphor or simile drawn from nature or ordinary life, which catches the hearer by its vividness or strangeness and leaves enough doubt about its exact application to provoke the mind into active thought. The last part of that definition is the key. A parable is not an illustration that decorates a point already made. It is a way of drawing hearers into a story so that they reach a judgment, often about themselves, before they realize it.

Jesus did not invent the parable. The Old Testament contains several, and the most famous shows exactly how a parable works. After David's adultery with Bathsheba and the murder of Uriah, the prophet Nathan tells the king a story about a rich man with many flocks who took a poor man's one beloved ewe lamb to serve to a guest (2 Samuel 12:1-4). David, outraged, pronounces that the rich man deserves to die. Nathan answers: “You are that man!” (2 Samuel 12:7). The story has led David to condemn himself. He could have defended himself against a direct accusation; he cannot defend himself against his own verdict.

Other Old Testament parables include Jotham's fable of the trees looking for a king (Judges 9:7-15), the story the wise woman of Tekoa tells David to bring Absalom home (2 Samuel 14:1-20), King Jehoash's taunt about a thistle and a cedar (2 Kings 14:9), Isaiah's song of the vineyard, which ends by revealing that the vineyard that yielded bad grapes is Israel (Isaiah 5:1-7), and Ezekiel's extended allegories of eagles, vines, and unfaithful sisters (Ezekiel 16, 17, 23). God tells Ezekiel to “pose a riddle; speak a parable to the house of Israel” (Ezekiel 17:2), and Psalm 78, which Matthew quotes to explain Jesus' use of parables, opens, “I will open my mouth in parables” (Psalm 78:2; Matthew 13:35).

The Jewish rabbis also taught in parables, called meshalim, and hundreds survive in the Talmud and the collections of midrash (interpretation of Scripture). Many begin ‘It is like a king who...’ and use the story to explain a verse of Scripture. They were written down later than the Gospels, but the form is clearly older, and scholars such as David Stern (Parables in Midrash, 1991) and Brad Young (Jesus and His Jewish Parables, 1989) have shown how much Jesus' parables share with them: stock figures such as kings, sons, servants, and vineyards; surprising turns; and the aim of moving the hearer to understanding and response. The difference most often noted is that the rabbinic parables usually serve to interpret Scripture, while Jesus' parables usually announce the kingdom of God and call for decision in the face of it.

Jesus' parables are drawn from the life his hearers lived: sowing and harvest, fishing, sheep, vineyards, baking, lost coins, debts, day laborers, absentee landlords, weddings, banquets, judges, and family quarrels over inheritance. The details are ordinary. The stories are not. Again and again, a parable takes an ordinary situation and gives it a twist that a first hearer would find surprising or scandalous. The hero of the story about who is a neighbor is a Samaritan, a member of a people most Jews of the day despised. A father runs to meet his disgraced son and throws a feast for him. A vineyard owner pays workers who worked one hour the same as those who worked all day. A shepherd leaves ninety-nine sheep to find one. A seed as small as a mustard seed becomes a tree. The twist is usually where the parable's meaning lies.

Most of the parables are about the kingdom of God, God's reign breaking into the world in Jesus' own ministry. Mark sums up Jesus' preaching with the announcement that the time is fulfilled and “the kingdom of God is near” (Mark 1:15), and the parables describe what that kingdom is like: hidden and small now, great at the end (the mustard seed and the leaven); worth everything (the treasure and the pearl); growing by God's power, not human effort (the seed growing secretly, Mark 4:26-29); gathering the unexpected (the great banquet); and bringing judgment as well as grace (the wheat and weeds, the net, the ten virgins).

Many parables are addressed to particular audiences and should be read with that audience in mind. Luke introduces the three parables of the lost sheep, the lost coin, and the lost son by saying that tax collectors and sinners were gathering to hear Jesus and that the Pharisees and scribes grumbled, “This man welcomes sinners and eats with them.” (Luke 15:2). The three stories answer that complaint, and the last one ends with the elder brother outside the party, his father pleading with him, and no word of how he responds. The grumblers are invited to see themselves in him and to finish the story. Luke introduces the parable of the Pharisee and the tax collector as told “To some who trusted in their own righteousness and viewed others with contempt” (Luke 18:9). And after the parable of the tenants who kill the owner's son, the religious leaders “knew that He had spoken this parable against them” (Mark 12:12).

The parables often end with a question or an open challenge rather than an explanation. The Good Samaritan is told in answer to a lawyer's question, “And who is my neighbor?” (Luke 10:29). Jesus ends with a different question, “Which of these three do you think was a neighbor to the man who fell into the hands of robbers?” (10:36), and when the lawyer answers, tells him, “Go and do likewise.” (10:37). The question has turned from whom I must love to what kind of neighbor I must be.

sections.h: The hard saying: parables that conceal
sections.body:
After the parable of the sower, Mark records one of the most difficult sayings in the Gospels. Jesus tells his disciples: “The mystery of the kingdom of God has been given to you, but to those on the outside everything is expressed in parables, so that, ‘they may be ever seeing but never perceiving, and ever hearing but never understanding; otherwise they might turn and be forgiven.’” (Mark 4:11-12). The quotation comes from Isaiah 6:9-10, where God commissions Isaiah to preach to a people whose hearts will be hardened by his message. Did Jesus tell parables in order to keep people from understanding?

Interpreters have answered in several ways. Many note that Matthew's parallel reads ‘because’ rather than ‘so that’ (Matthew 13:13): Jesus speaks in parables because people are not seeing and hearing, and the parables confirm a blindness already present. Some scholars, beginning with T. W. Manson (The Teaching of Jesus, 1931), suggested that Mark's Greek reflects an ambiguous Aramaic word that could mean ‘who’ as well as ‘so that’. Others take Mark's words at full strength and set them within the larger biblical pattern in which God's word both softens and hardens: the same message that opens the eyes of those who receive it closes the eyes of those who refuse it, as it did in Isaiah's day. On this reading parables are a form of judgment on the unwilling and of grace to the willing; they reward those who come closer and ask, as the disciples did, and they leave outside those who will not.

The context supports this. Mark says Jesus spoke to the crowds “to the extent that they could understand” (4:33) and explained everything privately to his disciples (4:34). The parables were not riddles designed to exclude, but they did require a response: “He who has ears to hear, let him hear.” (4:9). The dividing line between insiders and outsiders in Mark is not intelligence but willingness to come to Jesus and ask. Even the disciples do not understand at first (4:13); they are insiders because they ask.

The parables are unevenly spread across the Gospels, and each evangelist has his own collection. Mark has relatively few, gathered mostly in chapter 4 (the sower, the lamp, the growing seed, the mustard seed) with the tenants in chapter 12 and the fig tree in chapter 13. Matthew collects seven parables of the kingdom in chapter 13 and many parables of judgment and readiness in chapters 18 to 25, often introduced with ‘the kingdom of heaven is like’. Luke has the largest number found nowhere else, and they include many of the best known: the Good Samaritan, the friend at midnight, the rich fool, the lost coin, the lost son, the shrewd manager, the rich man and Lazarus, the persistent widow, and the Pharisee and the tax collector.

John contains no parables of the Synoptic kind, but uses extended figures, of the shepherd and the sheep (John 10) and the vine and the branches (John 15). John calls such speech a paroimia, a figure or veiled saying (10:6; 16:25). The Gospel of Thomas, a collection of sayings attributed to Jesus that survives complete in a Coptic manuscript found at Nag Hammadi in Egypt in 1945, contains versions of many Synoptic parables and some not found elsewhere. Scholars debate whether its versions are independent of the Gospels and early, or later and dependent on them; most date the collection in its present form to the second century.

The table lists the main parables and where they appear. Where two Gospels tell similar parables with significant differences (Matthew's wedding banquet and Luke's great banquet, Matthew's talents and Luke's minas), scholars debate whether they are two tellings of the same parable or two parables that Jesus, a traveling teacher, told on different occasions.

sections.body:
For most of Christian history, the parables were read as allegories, in which each detail stands for a spiritual reality. The practice has roots in the Gospels themselves: Jesus explains the sower detail by detail (the seed is the word, the birds are Satan, the rocky ground is those who fall away under persecution; Mark 4:13-20), and the wheat and weeds likewise (Matthew 13:36-43). The church fathers extended the method to every parable. The best-known example is Augustine's reading of the Good Samaritan in his Questions on the Gospels (2.19), from about AD 400: the man going down from Jerusalem to Jericho is Adam, Jerusalem the heavenly city from which he fell, Jericho (whose name was associated with the moon) our mortality, the robbers the devil and his angels, the priest and Levite the ministry of the Old Testament that could not save, the Samaritan Christ, the inn the church, and the innkeeper the apostle Paul. Origen, two centuries earlier, had offered a similar reading. Every word of such an interpretation teaches something true, and the reading was widely loved for a thousand years. But none of it is what the parable itself is about. It answers a question the lawyer did not ask and ignores the one he did.

The Reformers began to push back. John Calvin, in his commentary on the harmony of the Gospels, rejected the allegorical reading of the Good Samaritan as having no basis in the text and insisted on the parable's plain point about loving one's neighbor, though neither Calvin nor Luther abandoned allegory entirely elsewhere.

The decisive break came with the German scholar Adolf Jülicher, whose two-volume Die Gleichnisreden Jesu (The Parables of Jesus) appeared between the late 1880s and 1899. Jülicher argued that Jesus' parables were not allegories at all but extended similes, each making a single point of comparison; the allegorical explanations in the Gospels, he thought, were additions by the early church. His work freed the parables from centuries of imported meanings. But his single points tended to be broad moral generalities, such as the value of wise preparation or the importance of love, and critics have noted that a teacher crucified for his message is unlikely to have been put to death for teaching such truisms.

In the twentieth century, scholars tried to recover the point of each parable in the setting of Jesus' own ministry. C. H. Dodd's The Parables of the Kingdom (1935) read the parables as announcing that the kingdom of God had already arrived in Jesus, a view he called realized eschatology. Joachim Jeremias, in Die Gleichnisse Jesu (1947, translated as The Parables of Jesus), built on Dodd and on detailed knowledge of Palestinian life to reconstruct what he took to be the original form and setting of each parable, separating it from what he regarded as the early church's adaptations; he spoke of an eschatology in the process of being realized, the kingdom arriving but not yet complete. Jeremias's work remained standard for a generation, and his attention to the social world of the parables is still valuable, though scholars have since questioned how confidently the original can be separated from the Gospel versions.

From the 1960s, literary approaches treated the parables as works of art that do something to their hearers rather than simply convey a point. Scholars of the so-called new hermeneutic, such as Ernst Fuchs, spoke of the parables as language events. Robert Funk (Language, Hermeneutic, and Word of God, 1966), Dan Otto Via (The Parables, 1967), and John Dominic Crossan (In Parables, 1973) stressed how the parables subvert their hearers' expectations and overturn their world. Kenneth Bailey, drawing on decades of life in the Middle East, read the parables in light of village culture in Poet and Peasant (1976) and Through Peasant Eyes (1980), showing, for example, how shameful it would have been for a dignified father to run through the village to meet a son who had wished him dead. William Herzog (Parables as Subversive Speech, 1994) read several parables as exposing the economic oppression of first-century Galilee.

More recently, scholars have returned to questions Jülicher thought he had settled. Craig Blomberg (Interpreting the Parables, 1990) argued that the parables do contain allegorical elements and that a parable typically makes one main point for each main character, so that the prodigal son teaches about the father's grace, the younger son's repentance, and the elder son's resentment. Klyne Snodgrass (Stories with Intent, 2008) argued that the sharp line between parable and allegory is modern, that ancient parables, Jewish ones included, freely used analogy, and that the task is to find the analogy the story itself sets up, no more and no less. Amy-Jill Levine, a Jewish New Testament scholar (Short Stories by Jesus, 2014), warned against readings that make the parables work by caricaturing Judaism, for instance by assuming the priest and Levite passed by because of purity laws, and urged readers to hear the parables as a first-century Jewish audience would have heard them, with all their provocation intact.

The history of interpretation suggests some habits. First, read the setting. Notice who the parable is told to and why: Luke 15's grumbling Pharisees, the lawyer testing Jesus in Luke 10, the disciples asking for instruction in Mark 4. Many parables are answers to questions or responses to objections, and the setting often tells you the question.

Second, learn the world. A denarius was a day's wage for a laborer. Leaven, in Jewish usage, often stood for corruption, so a parable comparing the kingdom to leaven that a woman hid in a large amount of flour (Luke 13:21) would have sounded startling. Shepherds were often regarded with suspicion. Samaritans and Jews had centuries of hostility. A good study Bible or commentary will supply what the first hearers knew without being told.

Third, find the twist, the point where the story does something unexpected. That is usually where it bites. Then ask who the main characters are and with whom the first hearers would have identified. A parable often lets its hearers identify with one character and then turns the tables, as Nathan's parable did with David.

Fourth, distinguish between details that carry meaning and details that simply make the story work. Not every element is a symbol; the Samaritan's oil, wine, and two denarii show the extravagance of his care, not the sacraments and the two testaments. But do not overcorrect: some details plainly do carry meaning, especially where they echo the Old Testament, as the vineyard in the parable of the tenants echoes Isaiah 5.

Fifth, let the parable keep its open ending and its demand. Many parables end without resolution because the hearer is meant to supply it. The elder brother is still outside the feast. The master's question to the grumbling workers, “Or are you envious because I am generous?” (Matthew 20:15), is left hanging for the hearers to answer. Parables are not puzzles to solve and put away but stories that go on asking. Jesus said that every scribe trained for the kingdom is like a homeowner who brings out of his storeroom “new treasures as well as old” (Matthew 13:52), and the parables have been doing that for every generation of readers.
